key_insight: Learning intermediate physical states (surface-current maps) with deep generative models, instead of generating device layouts directly, yields a more stable and reliable route for inverse design of tunable and stacked metasurfaces. This intermediate representation bridges physics and design, improving robustness and control.
problem_solved: Inverse design of metasurfaces is ill-posed and unstable when mapping targets straight to layouts, especially for tunable/stacked devices; the paper addresses instability and poor generalization by introducing a physics-aware intermediate representation.
method: Train deep generative models to predict intermediate surface-current maps conditioned on desired electromagnetic responses.
Use the learned surface-current maps as a physics-grounded bridge to derive physical layouts (and to enable tuning/stacking) instead of directly generating geometry.
Integrate forward physics evaluation (or physics-aware loss) to ensure the intermediate maps map consistently to the target responses and manufacturable layouts.
impact: Provides AI/ML practitioners a general strategy for physics-driven inverse design: using intermediate physical states can improve stability, interpretability, and transferability of generative models across complex, tunable physical systems.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram: target response → generative model → surface-current map (intermediate) → layout → forward simulation

paper_title: Learning intermediate physical states for inverse metasurface design
